title: Neoplasms of Blood and Lymphoid Tissue
subject: Hematologic and Lymphoreticular System (HEME)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the clonal neoplasms of blood-forming and lymphoid cells: the acute and chronic leukemias, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, T cell lymphomas, plasma cell neoplasms, myelodysplastic syndromes, primary myelofibrosis, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, ending with tumor lysis syndrome. Each disease is explained from its cell of origin and its driving mutation, because those two facts predict the smear, the immunophenotype, the organs involved, and the complications. Board questions usually give an age, a smear finding, a marker, or a translocation and ask you to name the neoplasm or predict what it will do next, so the emphasis here is on reasoning from mechanism to finding.
prerequisites: Hematopoiesis: myeloid and lymphoid lineages and their maturation stages

Proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and how translocations activate oncogenes
Bone remodeling: RANKL, osteoprotegerin, osteoclasts, and osteoblasts
Coagulation cascade, fibrinolysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (HE-9-C)

blocks.text: Acute leukemias arise when mutations both block differentiation and allow continued proliferation, so immature blasts accumulate in the marrow. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a neoplasm of lymphoid precursors (lymphoblasts). It is the most common cancer of childhood, peaking at about 2 to 5 years of age, and about 85% of cases are precursor B cell tumors; the rest are precursor T cell tumors.

The defining marker is terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), the enzyme that adds random nucleotides at gene segment junctions during immunoglobulin and T cell receptor rearrangement. Because normally only early lymphoid precursors express it, nuclear TdT identifies a lymphoblast and separates ALL from mature lymphoid neoplasms such as CLL or Burkitt lymphoma. B-ALL blasts are usually CD19 and CD10 positive; T-ALL blasts express CD3 and other T cell markers and commonly present in adolescent males as a mediastinal (thymic) mass that can compress the airway or superior vena cava. Lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase negative and lack Auer rods.

The clinical picture follows from marrow replacement. Crowding of normal precursors causes anemia (fatigue, pallor), thrombocytopenia (petechiae, bleeding), and neutropenia (fever, infection). Expansion of the marrow cavity and periosteal infiltration cause bone pain and tenderness, which may make a child limp or refuse to walk. Blasts also infiltrate lymph nodes, liver, and spleen.

The central nervous system and testes are sanctuary sites: the blood-brain and blood-testis barriers exclude many drugs, so blasts there survive and cause relapse. CNS involvement presents with headache, vomiting, or cranial nerve palsies. Down syndrome raises ALL risk roughly 10 to 20 times. Cytogenetics carries prognosis: hyperdiploidy and t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 are favorable childhood findings, while t(9;22) BCR-ABL1, more common in adults, is unfavorable.

sections.title: Acute myeloid leukemia and acute promyelocytic leukemia

blocks.text: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a neoplasm of myeloid precursors that accumulate as myeloblasts. It is mainly a disease of adults, with a median age near 65 to 70 years. The traditional diagnostic threshold is at least 20% blasts in marrow or blood; certain defining genetic lesions, such as t(15;17), establish AML at lower blast counts. Cytopenias produce the same anemia, bleeding, and infection seen in ALL. Monocytic subtypes infiltrate gums and skin, and very high blast counts can cause leukostasis in lung and brain vessels.

Myeloid identity is shown by myeloperoxidase (MPO) positivity and by Auer rods, which are crystallized primary granules. Auer rods are never seen in normal cells or in ALL, so one rod in a blast establishes myeloid lineage.

Risk factors share one theme, damage to hematopoietic stem cell DNA: prior alkylating chemotherapy, topoisomerase II inhibitors, ionizing radiation, and benzene exposure. Myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative neoplasms progress to AML by acquiring further mutations. Down syndrome raises AML risk, most strikingly acute megakaryoblastic leukemia before about age 5, often with GATA1 mutations.
Acute promyelocytic leukemia and DIC

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) carries t(15;17), which fuses PML to the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene (RARA). The fusion protein represses genes that retinoic acid normally switches on, so cells arrest at the promyelocyte stage. The promyelocytes are packed with granules and often many Auer rods. Their tissue factor activates coagulation, and annexin II on their surface speeds plasmin generation, so APL produces DIC with prominent fibrinolysis. Patients can bleed catastrophically, and DIC can worsen as cells break down. Pharmacologic doses of all-trans retinoic acid overcome the block and force maturation, which confirms the mechanism. For these reasons APL is a hematologic emergency.

blocks.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a neoplasm of small, mature-appearing B cells and is the most common leukemia of adults in Western countries, with a median age near 70. When the same cells are mainly in lymph nodes rather than blood, the disease is called small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL). Many patients are asymptomatic and are found because a routine count shows an absolute lymphocytosis. Others present with painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or infections.

The immunophenotype is distinctive. CLL cells express the B cell markers CD19 and CD20 (dimly) and surface immunoglobulin at low levels, and they coexpress CD5, normally a T cell marker, together with CD23. CD5 also appears on mantle cell lymphoma, but mantle cell lymphoma is CD23 negative, which separates the two. On the smear, CLL cells are fragile and are crushed by the spreading slide, leaving smudge cells.

The complications come from immune dysregulation rather than marrow crowding alone. Normal B cell function is suppressed, so hypogammaglobulinemia is common, with recurrent bacterial infections, often by encapsulated organisms. At the same time tolerance fails: nonneoplastic B cells produce IgG autoantibodies against red cells, causing warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia with a positive direct antiglobulin test and spherocytes, and less often immune thrombocytopenia.

CLL is indolent, but in a small minority of patients (roughly 2% to 10%) the clone acquires further mutations and undergoes Richter transformation, most often to diffuse large B cell lymphoma. Transformation is suggested by a rapidly enlarging node, fever, weight loss, and a rising LDH, and it carries a poor prognosis.

blocks.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm of a pluripotent stem cell, usually presenting in adults aged about 40 to 60. Its defining lesion is t(9;22), which joins BCR on chromosome 22 to ABL1 on chromosome 9. The shortened chromosome 22 is the Philadelphia chromosome. The fusion protein is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives growth factor-independent proliferation through RAS and other signaling pathways.

Unlike the acute leukemias, maturation is preserved in chronic phase, so the blood fills with granulocytes at every stage: myelocytes and metamyelocytes predominate over blasts, alongside band and segmented neutrophils. Basophilia and eosinophilia are typical, and platelets are often high. The spleen enlarges, sometimes massively, from extramedullary hematopoiesis and leukemic infiltration, causing left upper quadrant fullness or early satiety. Symptoms are often mild fatigue and weight loss.

The main differential is a leukemoid reaction, a reactive neutrophilia from severe infection or inflammation. Basophilia and splenomegaly favor CML, and a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score has historically supported CML, but diagnosis is confirmed only by detecting t(9;22) by karyotype or FISH, or the BCR-ABL1 transcript by RT-PCR. Its presence also predicts response to drugs that inhibit the ABL1 kinase, which shows how completely the disease depends on this one enzyme.

Without control, CML progresses. Genomic instability adds mutations that block maturation, moving the disease into an accelerated phase (rising blasts and basophils, worsening counts and spleen size) and then blast crisis, in which 20% or more blasts make it behave as acute leukemia. About two thirds of blast crises are myeloid and one third lymphoid, reflecting the stem cell origin.

blocks.text: Hairy cell leukemia is an uncommon, indolent neoplasm of mature B cells, typically in middle-aged men (median age about 55, men affected about four to five times as often as women). It is named for fine hairlike cytoplasmic projections seen on the smear and on electron microscopy. Nearly all classic cases carry the BRAF V600E mutation, which constantly activates the MAPK pathway and is a useful diagnostic marker.

The cells have a characteristic phenotype. They are B cells (CD19, CD20) that also express CD11c, CD25, and CD103, along with annexin A1. Historically they were identified by tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining, which is still tested even though flow cytometry has largely replaced it.

The distribution of hairy cells explains the clinical picture. They home to the bone marrow, the splenic red pulp, and the liver, rather than to lymph nodes. In the marrow they induce a fine reticulin fibrosis that traps cells, so aspiration yields a dry tap and a core biopsy is needed. In the spleen they fill the red pulp, producing massive splenomegaly, while lymphadenopathy is characteristically absent. Marrow infiltration and splenic sequestration together cause pancytopenia, and monocytopenia is a typical clue. Infections, including atypical mycobacterial infections, follow from the loss of monocytes and neutrophils.

blocks.title: Chronic leukemias compared
blocks.caption: A chronic leukemia is identified by its cell of origin, its marker, and where the cells settle.

blocks.text: Lymphomas are neoplasms of lymphocytes that form masses, usually in lymph nodes. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is unusual because the neoplastic cells, Reed-Sternberg cells and their mononuclear variants, make up only a small fraction of the tumor. A Reed-Sternberg cell is large, with two mirror-image nuclei or nuclear lobes, each with a prominent inclusion-like nucleolus. It derives from a germinal center B cell that has lost most of its B cell program, so it is typically CD15 and CD30 positive, CD45 negative, and usually CD20 negative. Its cytokines recruit reactive lymphocytes, eosinophils, histiocytes, and fibroblasts, which form most of the mass.

Hodgkin lymphoma usually begins in a single node group, often cervical or mediastinal, and spreads in an orderly way to adjacent groups through lymphatics. This contiguous spread means it is often localized at diagnosis and that anatomic stage predicts behavior well; extranodal and leukemic disease is uncommon. Age distribution is bimodal, with a peak in young adults and a second in older adults. EBV is present in the tumor cells of a substantial fraction of cases, most often the mixed cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted types. Cytokines from the tumor and its reactive background produce B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, and loss of more than 10% of body weight over 6 months).

blocks.text: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHL) are a varied group, most of B cell origin, in which the neoplastic cells form most of the mass. They often involve several noncontiguous node groups, including mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring, and frequently arise in or spread to extranodal sites such as the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and central nervous system. Many also enter the marrow and blood. For this reason anatomic stage carries less prognostic weight than histologic type.

blocks.text: Many B cell lymphomas carry a translocation that moves an oncogene next to an immunoglobulin locus, most often the heavy chain locus (IGH) on chromosome 14. B cells drive their immunoglobulin genes very hard, so the moved oncogene is overexpressed. The function of that oncogene sets the tumor's behavior.

Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common NHL, about a quarter to a third of cases. Sheets of large B cells efface the node. It usually presents in older adults as a rapidly enlarging nodal or extranodal mass and is aggressive. It can arise de novo or by transformation of follicular lymphoma or CLL. Rearrangements of BCL6 are common.

Follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18), which places the anti-apoptotic gene BCL2 under IGH control. Cells survive when they should die, so the tumor grows slowly by accumulation, forming crowded back-to-back follicles. It is indolent, with painless lymphadenopathy that may wax and wane, but it is rarely cured and can transform to DLBCL. In normal germinal centers BCL2 is off, so BCL2 staining of follicles separates follicular lymphoma from reactive hyperplasia.

Burkitt lymphoma carries t(8;14), placing MYC under IGH control (variants pair MYC with light chain loci). MYC drives cell cycle entry and growth, so nearly every cell is dividing; it is among the fastest-growing human tumors. Many cells die, and macrophages that ingest them appear as pale spaces among dark tumor cells, the starry sky pattern. The endemic African form, almost always EBV positive, presents as a jaw or facial mass in children; the sporadic form presents as an abdominal mass, often ileocecal.

Mantle cell lymphoma carries t(11;14), overexpressing cyclin D1, which pushes cells from G1 into S phase. It is CD5 positive like CLL but CD23 negative, occurs in older men, and is aggressive, often with GI involvement (lymphomatous polyposis). MALT lymphoma, an extranodal marginal zone lymphoma, arises where chronic inflammation has created lymphoid tissue: the stomach with Helicobacter pylori, salivary glands in Sjogren syndrome, and thyroid in Hashimoto thyroiditis. Early gastric MALT lymphoma depends on H. pylori-driven T cell help and can regress after the infection is eradicated.

sections.title: T cell lymphomas: adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma and mycosis fungoides

blocks.text: Peripheral T cell lymphomas are neoplasms of mature, post-thymic T cells and are far less common than B cell lymphomas in Western countries. Two are emphasized for boards because each is defined by a clear mechanism.

Adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a neoplasm of CD4 T cells caused by human T cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), a retrovirus endemic in southern Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America, and West Africa. It spreads through breast milk, sexual contact, and blood. The viral Tax protein activates host transcription factors such as NF-kappaB and drives T cell proliferation; after decades of infection, a small fraction of carriers (a few percent) develop ATLL. The cells are CD4 and CD25 positive and often have multilobed flower-shaped nuclei. Typical features are skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphocytosis, hypercalcemia, and lytic bone lesions. Tumor cells secrete PTH-related protein and express RANKL, both of which activate osteoclasts. The acute form is aggressive.

Mycosis fungoides is a neoplasm of skin-homing CD4 T cells, the most common cutaneous T cell lymphoma. The cells carry homing receptors that direct them to the skin and infiltrate the epidermis (epidermotropism), where they cluster as Pautrier microabscesses, which are collections of atypical lymphocytes rather than true abscesses. Their nuclei are folded and cerebriform. Disease progresses slowly over years from eczema-like patches to plaques and then tumors. When the clone spreads to the blood, the circulating cells are called Sezary cells; Sezary syndrome is the combination of generalized erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and Sezary cells in the blood.

sections.title: Multiple myeloma: from clonal plasma cells to end-organ damage

blocks.text: Multiple myeloma is a neoplasm of plasma cells, the terminally differentiated B cells that secrete antibody. It occurs mainly in older adults and is about twice as common in Black as in White Americans. The clone grows in the marrow, depends on IL-6 from marrow stromal cells, and secretes a single immunoglobulin or light chain in enormous amounts. On serum protein electrophoresis this monoclonal protein forms a narrow M spike in the gamma region, most often IgG, next most often IgA, and in about a fifth of cases free light chains only. Normal polyclonal immunoglobulin falls.

Bone disease is the most characteristic damage. Myeloma cells raise RANKL and lower osteoprotegerin, the decoy receptor that normally neutralizes RANKL, so osteoclasts are activated. They also inhibit osteoblasts, partly through DKK1, a blocker of Wnt signaling. Resorption without new bone formation produces punched-out lytic lesions, most often in the skull, spine, ribs, and pelvis, with pathologic fractures and hypercalcemia. Because osteoblasts are inactive, serum alkaline phosphatase is usually normal and radionuclide bone scans often miss the lesions.

Free light chains are small enough to be filtered. They overwhelm proximal tubular reabsorption, appear in urine as Bence Jones protein (which routine dipsticks, sensitive mainly to albumin, miss), and in the distal nephron bind uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) to form obstructing, inflammatory casts. This light chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcemia, and dehydration all contribute to renal failure.

Anemia, usually normocytic, results from marrow replacement, inflammatory cytokines, and reduced erythropoietin from injured kidneys. The high concentration of serum protein reduces the charge that normally keeps red cells apart, so they stack as rouleaux and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate rises. Infections, especially with encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, follow from the loss of functional antibody. Hypercalcemia, renal injury, anemia, and bone lesions (CRAB) are the end-organ features that define symptomatic myeloma.

sections.title: MGUS, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, and AL amyloidosis

blocks.text: An M protein does not by itself mean myeloma. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a small clonal plasma cell population that produces a modest M protein without damaging organs. It is common, present in about 3% of people over 50 and more with age. The defining limits are an M protein below 3 g/dL, fewer than 10% clonal plasma cells in the marrow, and no CRAB features or other myeloma-defining biomarkers (such as 60% or more marrow plasma cells). MGUS progresses to myeloma or a related disorder at about 1% per year, so it is a premalignant state. Smoldering myeloma sits between them: a higher M protein or 10% to 60% marrow plasma cells, still without end-organ damage.

Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, a B cell neoplasm with cells ranging from small lymphocytes to plasma cells, that secretes monoclonal IgM. Most cases carry the MYD88 L265P mutation. IgM is a pentamer of about 900 kDa that largely stays in the vessels, so a high level raises plasma viscosity. Hyperviscosity slows flow in small vessels, causing blurred vision with dilated, segmented retinal veins, headache, dizziness, confusion, and mucosal bleeding from impaired platelet function. Because the cell is lymphoplasmacytic, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are common, while lytic lesions and hypercalcemia are characteristically absent.

AL amyloidosis results when a plasma cell clone, often small, secretes light chains, usually lambda, that misfold into beta-pleated sheet fibrils. The fibrils deposit in the kidney (nephrotic syndrome), heart (restrictive cardiomyopathy with low voltage on ECG), tongue (macroglossia), nerves (peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome), and vessel walls (periorbital purpura). Tissue stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. AL amyloidosis can occur alone or with myeloma.

rows: IgG or IgA most often; below 3 g/dL
IgG or IgA, or light chains only
blocks.caption: The protein class, the plasma cell burden, and the presence or absence of end-organ damage separate the three disorders.

blocks.title: Worked example: classifying a monoclonal protein
blocks.text: Patient A has an IgG M protein of 1.4 g/dL, 6% marrow plasma cells, normal calcium, creatinine, and hemoglobin, and no bone lesions. All three MGUS criteria are met, so this is MGUS. Patient B has IgG 4.2 g/dL, 30% plasma cells, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, and vertebral lytic lesions. The plasma cell burden exceeds 10% and there are CRAB features (anemia, bone lesions), so this is multiple myeloma. Patient C has an IgM spike of 3.5 g/dL, blurred vision, epistaxis, enlarged nodes, and a normal skeletal survey. IgM, hyperviscosity, nodal disease, and absent lytic lesions point to Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. The class of protein and the type of organ damage decide the diagnosis, not the size of the spike alone.

Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are clonal stem cell neoplasms in which hematopoiesis is both abnormal in appearance (dysplastic) and ineffective. Most patients are older adults, with a median age near 70. Therapy-related MDS follows alkylating agents or radiation, usually after a latency of several years, and often shows loss of chromosome 5 or 7 material; benzene exposure is another recognized risk.

The central paradox is a marrow that is usually normocellular or hypercellular in a patient with low blood counts. The clone produces many precursors, but they are defective and undergo apoptosis in the marrow before release. This intramedullary death is what ineffective hematopoiesis means. Patients therefore present with cytopenias: macrocytic or normocytic anemia, neutropenia with infections, and thrombocytopenia with bleeding. Many are found because an unexplained macrocytic anemia does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate.

Dysplasia is visible in each lineage. Pseudo-Pelger-Huet neutrophils have bilobed nuclei (or nonsegmented nuclei) and often reduced granules, resembling the inherited Pelger-Huet anomaly but acquired. Ringed sideroblasts are erythroid precursors whose iron-laden mitochondria encircle the nucleus, seen on Prussian blue stain; they reflect defective heme synthesis and are strongly associated with SF3B1 splicing factor mutations. Megakaryocytes are small with hypolobated nuclei, and erythroid precursors may look megaloblastoid.

MDS is defined by fewer than 20% marrow blasts. Additional mutations raise the blast count, and about a third of patients progress to AML, which carries a poor prognosis. Many others die of the cytopenias themselves, through infection or bleeding, before transformation occurs. Isolated deletion of 5q is a distinct, more favorable subtype, typically in older women, with macrocytic anemia and normal or high platelets.

blocks.caption: Dysplasia in one or more lineages, cytopenias, and a cellular marrow together define MDS.

blocks.text: Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm, a relative of polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, in which the marrow becomes progressively scarred. Its driver mutations all keep JAK-STAT signaling switched on without growth factor: JAK2 V617F in about half to 60% of cases, CALR in about a quarter, and MPL (the thrombopoietin receptor) in about 5% to 10%. A small fraction has none of the three.

The fibrosis is reactive and is driven by neoplastic megakaryocytes. These cells proliferate in atypical clusters and release growth factors, including platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta), that stimulate normal fibroblasts to lay down reticulin and then collagen. The bone may become sclerotic. In an early prefibrotic phase the marrow is hypercellular and platelet counts may be high, but as scarring advances the marrow can no longer support hematopoiesis.

Hematopoiesis then shifts to the spleen and liver, where it took place in fetal life. This extramedullary hematopoiesis produces massive splenomegaly, with early satiety and left upper quadrant discomfort, and hepatomegaly; portal hypertension can follow. Marrow fibrosis makes aspiration fail, a dry tap, so diagnosis requires a core biopsy. Red cells squeezed through scarred marrow and released from extramedullary sites are deformed into teardrop cells (dacrocytes), and the loss of marrow architecture releases nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes, producing a leukoerythroblastic smear. Anemia is the typical count abnormality, with variable white cell and platelet counts. High cell turnover raises uric acid and LDH, and constitutional symptoms are common. A minority of patients transform to AML.

blocks.text: Teardrop cells and a leukoerythroblastic picture are not specific. Marrow infiltration by metastatic carcinoma, granulomas, or other neoplasms (myelophthisis) produces the same smear, and secondary fibrosis can follow polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia, so the diagnosis rests on marrow biopsy and mutation testing.

Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells of the epidermis and mucosa. Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a clonal proliferation of cells with the Langerhans cell phenotype, now regarded as a myeloid neoplasm because many cases carry activating mutations of the MAPK pathway, most often BRAF V600E (in about half). The lesional cells have abundant pale cytoplasm and grooved, folded nuclei, and they are usually mixed with many eosinophils.

The cells are identified by immunostaining and ultrastructure. They express CD1a, S100, and langerin (CD207). Langerin is the protein that forms Birbeck granules, rod-shaped cytoplasmic structures with a dilated end that gives them a tennis racket shape on electron microscopy.

Presentation depends on how widely the cells spread, and it is mainly a disease of children. Unifocal disease, called eosinophilic granuloma, is a single lytic bone lesion, most often in the skull, femur, vertebra, or rib, in an older child or young adult. It causes local pain, swelling, or a pathologic fracture, and can regress spontaneously. Multifocal bone disease may involve the skull base and orbit and the pituitary stalk. Infiltration of the stalk or posterior pituitary interrupts ADH delivery, causing central diabetes insipidus with polyuria and polydipsia. Multisystem disease, usually in children under about 2 years, involves skin (a scaly, seborrheic-like eruption), liver, spleen, lymph nodes, lungs, and marrow; marrow involvement causes cytopenias, and the course can be aggressive.

blocks.title: Clinical patterns of LCH
rows: Single lytic bone lesion, often skull; pain or fracture
Several lytic lesions, skull base and orbit; diabetes insipidus
Skin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, lung disease, cytopenias
blocks.caption: The same CD1a and S100 positive cell causes a single bone lesion or widespread disease, depending on extent.

blocks.text: Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is the metabolic consequence of releasing the contents of a very large number of tumor cells into the blood faster than the kidneys can clear them. It usually begins within about 12 to 72 hours after cytotoxic therapy starts, and it can occur spontaneously in tumors with very high turnover. Risk is greatest with a large, rapidly dividing, treatment-sensitive tumor: Burkitt lymphoma, ALL and AML with high white counts, and other bulky aggressive lymphomas. Preexisting kidney disease, dehydration, and a high pretreatment uric acid or LDH increase risk.

Each abnormality follows from what cells contain. Potassium is the main intracellular cation, so hyperkalemia appears early and is the most immediately dangerous change, causing peaked T waves, conduction block, and ventricular arrhythmias. Phosphate is concentrated in cells (malignant lymphoblasts carry even more than normal lymphocytes), so hyperphosphatemia follows. Phosphate binds calcium and precipitates as calcium phosphate, lowering ionized calcium; the resulting hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability (paresthesias, tetany, seizures) and prolongs the QT interval. Nucleic acids are broken down, and their purines are converted by xanthine oxidase, through hypoxanthine and xanthine, to uric acid, giving hyperuricemia.

The kidney is injured by crystals. Uric acid has a pKa of about 5.5, so in the acidic, concentrated fluid of the distal tubules and collecting ducts it exists largely as poorly soluble uric acid and crystallizes. Calcium phosphate also deposits in tubules and interstitium. The resulting acute kidney injury reduces excretion of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, which raises them further, a self-reinforcing cycle.

blocks.title: The renal cycle in tumor lysis syndrome
steps: Tumor cells lyse and release K+, phosphate, and purines
Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystallize in tubules
Acute kidney injury lowers excretion
Serum K+, phosphate, and uric acid rise further
blocks.caption: Kidney injury both results from and amplifies the metabolic abnormalities.

blocks.title: Laboratory pattern in tumor lysis syndrome
rows: Further retention of K+ and phosphate
blocks.caption: Four of the five values rise; calcium is the one that falls, because it is consumed by phosphate.

blocks.title: Worked example: predicting the labs
blocks.text: A 9-year-old boy with a large abdominal Burkitt lymphoma starts chemotherapy. Thirty-six hours later he has muscle cramps and reduced urine output. Start from cell contents. Massive lysis releases potassium, so expect potassium above about 6 mEq/L with peaked T waves. Released phosphate rises and binds calcium, so phosphate is high and total and ionized calcium are low; the cramps are hypocalcemic tetany. Released purines become uric acid, which crystallizes in acidic tubular fluid, and calcium phosphate deposits as well, so creatinine rises and urine output falls. Reduced filtration then retains more potassium and phosphate. The only value that falls is calcium, and the most urgent threat is the potassium.

integration.text: Across these neoplasms the same few principles predict almost everything. The cell of origin sets the markers and the sites involved: TdT marks precursor lymphoid cells, myeloperoxidase and Auer rods mark myeloid blasts, CD5 marks CLL and mantle cell lymphoma, CD15 and CD30 mark Reed-Sternberg cells, and plasma cells reveal themselves through the protein they secrete. The driver lesion sets the behavior: a block in maturation gives an acute leukemia, a constantly active tyrosine kinase with intact maturation gives a myeloproliferative neoplasm (CML, primary myelofibrosis), a block in apoptosis gives an indolent lymphoma, and forced cell division gives an aggressive one. Microbiology adds EBV, HTLV-1, and H. pylori as drivers of lymphocyte proliferation, and immunology explains why CLL and myeloma cause infections and autoimmunity.

Complications link these diseases to other systems. Marrow failure produces anemia, bleeding, and infection regardless of the cause, so cytopenias alone do not identify the neoplasm. Bone is attacked through RANKL in myeloma and ATLL and by direct infiltration in ALL and LCH; the kidney is injured by light chains, calcium, amyloid, and tumor lysis crystals; coagulation fails in APL; and the pituitary fails in LCH. Teardrop cells, a dry tap, or an M protein point toward a diagnosis but are shared by other conditions, so classification ultimately rests on morphology combined with immunophenotype and genetics, and diagnostic thresholds are revised as classification systems change.

summary: Acute leukemias combine blocked maturation with proliferation; TdT identifies ALL, and myeloperoxidase with Auer rods identifies AML.
APL with t(15;17) PML-RARA arrests cells at the promyelocyte stage, and their granules trigger DIC with marked fibrinolysis.
CLL is a CD5 and CD23 positive mature B cell neoplasm whose main harms are hypogammaglobulinemia, warm autoimmune hemolysis, and Richter transformation.
CML is driven by the BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase from t(9;22), shows all maturation stages with basophilia, and ends in blast crisis when maturation fails.
Hairy cell leukemia (TRAP, CD11c, CD103, BRAF V600E) homes to marrow and splenic red pulp, causing a dry tap, pancytopenia, and massive splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy.
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma has sparse CD15 and CD30 positive Reed-Sternberg cells and spreads contiguously; non-Hodgkin lymphoma spreads noncontiguously and often extranodally.
B cell lymphoma behavior follows the translocated gene: BCL2 in follicular lymphoma is indolent, MYC in Burkitt lymphoma is very fast, and cyclin D1 marks mantle cell lymphoma.
Myeloma cells activate osteoclasts through RANKL and suppress osteoblasts, causing lytic lesions and hypercalcemia; light chains form tubular casts and can form AL amyloid.
MGUS has an M protein below 3 g/dL, under 10% marrow plasma cells, and no organ damage; Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia secretes IgM, causing hyperviscosity without lytic lesions.
Tumor lysis releases K+, phosphate, and purines, producing hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and crystal-induced acute kidney injury.

Mutation frequencies (BRAF V600E in about half of LCH, JAK2 about 50% to 60%, CALR about 25%, MPL about 5% to 10% in primary myelofibrosis) and the Richter transformation rate (about 2% to 10%) vary among sources and are stated as approximate.
Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is rarely used now; confirm whether NABNE still tests a low LAP score as a CML finding.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the historical eponyms Letterer-Siwe disease and Hand-Schuller-Christian disease for LCH patterns; this chapter uses descriptive terms.
MGUS progression risk (about 1% per year) and prevalence (about 3% over age 50) are standard consensus figures; confirm the values NABNE uses.
